title: File Systems
body:
The on-disk structures that turn a flat array of numbered blocks into named
[[File|files]] in [[Directory|directories]]. Hardware gives you "block 4,192,006";
the file system is what lets you say `notes/3659.md` instead.

**This note is the implementation; [[File System Interface]] is the API.** Same split as
everywhere else in the vault: what it looks like from outside versus how it is built.

## What is on the disk

| Structure | Holds |
|---|---|
| Boot block | what to run at startup |
| Superblock | size, block size, where everything else is, free-space bookkeeping |
| Inode table | one record per file: size, owner, timestamps, permissions, **and where the blocks are** |
| Data blocks | the actual bytes |
| Directories | a file whose contents are (name → inode number) pairs |

A directory being just a file is the trick worth remembering. It means directories nest for
free, and it means the *name* of a file lives in its parent directory, not in the file. Two
names can point at one inode, which is what a hard link is.

## Allocating blocks to a file

| Scheme | How | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Contiguous | start block plus length | fast, but you must know the size up front and it fragments |
| Linked | each block stores the next block's number | no random access; seeking to the middle means walking there |
| Indexed | an index block lists every block of the file | one extra read, and the index block caps the file size |

Real Unix file systems use indexed with **multiple levels**: the inode holds a dozen direct
block pointers, then a pointer to a block of pointers, then a doubly indirect one. Small
files cost one lookup; huge files are still possible.

The same array-versus-pointer trade as [[Linked Structure]] in first year, decided again
one layer down.

## Why any of it is fast

Disk is slow enough that all of this is designed around avoiding it: the OS keeps a
**buffer cache** of recently used blocks in [[Main memory]] and reads ahead when access
looks sequential. That is [[Buffering]] and locality again, same argument as [[Cache]] and
[[Virtual Memory]] make one level up.
